title: Captain Ilya Ren and the Borrowed Horizon
body:
Signature fiction — unofficial continuation, not affiliated with or endorsed by the rights holders. Original characters and settings; no copyrighted text is reproduced.

Captain Ilya Ren had lived in the survey ship Wayfinder long enough to know which doors stuck in winter and which neighbours lied politely about it, and so when a compass rose cut from a single sheet of tin turned up, plain as a fact and impossible as a rumour, Captain Ilya Ren understood at once that ignoring it would cost more than chasing it. The morning after the discovery, the town's ordinary business went on as usual, which was itself the strangest part: bakers baked, ferries left on time, and nobody mentioned the thing that had changed the shape of the day. Captain Ilya Ren packed a bag, left a note that said only where the spare key was, and set out before courage could be talked out of the plan.

On the road Captain Ilya Ren met a street musician whose songs remember their singers, who joined the walk for reasons of their own and stayed for reasons they would only explain later, after the second river crossing. Together they traced the trouble to a mine owner damming the river of stories, whose scheme was tidy, profitable and quietly ruinous: it took something that belonged to everyone and charged everyone to use it. The confrontation was not a duel but a negotiation held in a room with no exits and too many witnesses, where Captain Ilya Ren laid out the evidence piece by piece — a receipt, a timetable, a letter in a familiar hand — until the scheme's tidiness unravelled in public. There was a moment, sharp as a snapped string, when the outcome could have gone either way, and Captain Ilya Ren chose the harder sentence over the easy silence.

What followed was repair rather than triumph: the taken thing was returned in instalments, apologies were made in the right order, and the town agreed on new rules written down where anyone could read them. Captain Ilya Ren came home changed in the small ways that matter — slower to promise, quicker to notice, fond of the ordinary morning light — and put a compass rose cut from a single sheet of tin on a shelf where it could do no more harm and no more good than an honest reminder. The story of Captain Ilya Ren and the Borrowed Horizon ends here, complete in itself, though the road out of the survey ship Wayfinder remains open, and another traveller may one day walk it for a different reason.
